Myanmar Reflects on 2016 Kyat Crisis and Its Aftermath for Trade and Industry

Yangon—Eight years after Myanmar’s 2016 currency crisis brought the kyat to historic lows, the country’s business community is taking stock of the economic shock’s long-term implications. In the second quarter of 2016, a rapid depreciation of the kyat saw the exchange rate plunge from 1,170 kyat to the US dollar in March to over 1,400 kyat by July, triggering widespread uncertainty across import-dependent sectors.

The crisis, spurred by a combination of falling foreign investment, a widening current account deficit, and declining export revenues—especially in the garment and agricultural sectors—strained cash flows for manufacturers and traders. "We saw costs for imported raw materials increase almost overnight by 20-25%," recalled U Ko Aung, secretary of the Myanmar Federation of Industries. "Many smaller workshops had to suspend operations or lay off workers."

Inflation surged to 11.5% by year-end, according to Central Bank data, affecting purchasing power and dampening consumer demand. The government responded with emergency measures, including foreign currency auctions and tighter monetary policy. The Central Bank of Myanmar raised its benchmark rate by 100 basis points in July 2016, and restricted large kyat withdrawals to stabilize the system.

"Stabilizing the kyat restored some business confidence, but it took over a year for trade volumes to recover," noted May Thiri Htun, an economist at Asia Market Insights. Exporters, particularly in rice and seafood, benefitted from the weaker currency in the short term, but most importers faced significant losses.

While the crisis abated in 2017, local businesses say its lessons remain relevant. "We are more cautious with our currency exposure today," said U Ko Aung. "The 2016 kyat crisis taught us the importance of hedging and preparing for volatility in global markets."
